newsitem.title: USA: US high-yield buyers look abroad to boost returns.
newsitem.headline: US high-yield buyers look abroad to boost returns.

text.p: Excess liquidity in the U.S. high-yield bond market is tempting more and more money managers to look to the emerging debt markets to bolster investor returns, according to analysts.

"Liquidity needs to find a place to go and the more liquidity there is, the more people will justify buying stuff that they may not have bought otherwise," said one emerging market fund manager at a major U.S. investment firm who requested anonymity.
Although movement by domestic high-yield money managers has been gradual, sources said hefty returns offered by emerging markets are clearly luring more investors overseas.

"For the last year or so, there has definitely been a search for yield overseas," said Rich Byrne, head of global high-yield research at Merrill Lynch & Co. "It's still relatively small but it is nice to find buyers from different places."
Returns on high-yield bonds, which are currently at historically tight spread levels, pale in comparison to that of emerging market debt instruments, sources said.

Gary Evans, senior emerging markets strategist at Lehman Brothers, said a BB-plus high yield credit will trade roughly 100 basis points tighter than that of an emerging market sovereign credit, and the lower-tiered credits will post even greater returns in excess of 200 basis points.
Since the beginning of the year, analysts said spreads on high-yield U.S. corporate bonds have narrowed by about 100 basis points because of strong demand.

Sources attributed the spread tightening in the high-yield sector to the surge in new issuance, which at the end of the third quarter had reached $47.9 billion. This exceeds the total for any prior year except 1993, when issuance measured a whopping $72.3 billion.

"Another reason why people are looking for alternatives is because we still have cash and there is still a perception that there is more demand than supply which has caused some of the relative value in the market to dissipate," said King Penniman, president of KDP Investor Advisors.
While emerging market debt instruments have also performed extremely well this year, sources said the returns were still much better than that of domestic high-yield bonds.

"Despite rapid spread compression over the past few months, the asset class (emerging market bonds) still appears cheap on a spread basis relative to comparably rated U.S. high-yield bonds," Evans added.
Indeed, emerging market debt issuance has increased both in the Yankee bond market and Eurobond market in order to meet the growing demand.

According to data compiled by Merrill Lynch, approximately $58.2 billion of emerging market corporate and sovereign debt has been issued and has settled as of October 31, 1996, exceeding 1995's record-high total of $36.3 billion.

The figures are comprised of all external debt issuance by emerging market countries, which includes Yankee bonds, Eurobond issues and Samurais among others. But the $58.2 billion through October, 1996, does not include an additional $3.3 billion in new bonds waiting to settle and another $10 billion expected to be priced before year end.

In compiling the data, Merrill said it included all emerging market corporate and sovereign debt issuance from countries that had a rating of BBB or less. The firm noted that the figures did not include issuance from Chile, China, Malaysia, Thailand, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, South Korea, and the Czech Republic.

The near doubling of emerging market debt issuance in one year reflects the impressive surge in demand. But sources noted that the higher premium paid to investors for emerging market debt issuance also reflects the extreme volatility and the many added risks inherent in these investments.
One high-yield analyst questioned how long traditional high-yield investors would be able to hold emerging market debt should a downturn in the market occur.

Unlike the U.S. high-yield market, risk factors that need to be considered by investors are sovereign risk, the different bankruptcy laws and legal systems, and the varying accounting rules within the different countries.

"The risks are an aspect of cross border investing, which you don't have when you invest in domestic markets. So, it ultimately boils down to investors' ability to get comfortable with our credits," said Peter Allen, head of emerging markets research at Bank of Boston.

Eventually though, sources said a growing sophistication and understanding of the emerging markets will provide even more traditional high-yield buyers the assurance of investing in these sectors despite the added risks.
